Shared weights: how one update reaches states you never visited

When states share a few weights, one update can teach states you never visited, and it can also blur two states together and move the target you're chasing.

Picture a cart on a track with a pole balanced on top. It has four sensors (cart position, cart speed, pole angle and pole angular speed) and two actions: push left or push right. The simplest way to learn values is a table. You chop each sensor into bins and keep one number for every combination of bins and action. Finer bins multiply the entries, and each entry still needs its own experience. That second part bugs me more. You can land in one bin a thousand times and the bin right next door still holds whatever number it started with.

So how does a learner get a value for a state it has never visited? It stops giving every state its own number. Instead we describe each state with a few numbers, called its features x(s), and predict its value with a weighted sum, v̂(s) = w⊤x(s) (the hat means "estimate"). To fit one state to a target y, we nudge the weights in the direction that shrinks its squared error: w ← w + α(y − v̂)x, where α is a small step size. Every state reads the same w, so one update can change predictions at states we never trained. Let's follow two cart states, A and B. To keep the arithmetic small, we'll describe each with just two made-up features: (1, 1) for A and (1, 2) for B. Start both weights at zero, train only on A, and watch what happens to B. If B gets more accurate, great. But what if it gets worse, or the target we're fitting starts to move?

Step ④ is the one I'd stare at. In TD learning (see the bootstrapping post), the target is the reward plus the discounted value of the next state, and that value comes from the same weights we're updating. We hold the target fixed while we take the gradient, which is why this is called a semi-gradient method (if you differentiate through the target you get a different update). The next time A → B comes up, though, the target gets recomputed, and our own update to A has already pushed it up. A table has no such coupling. Whether this drift settles or runs away depends on which experience you train on. If we collect it by following the policy whose values we're learning, there are convergence results for linear TD under technical assumptions (Sutton and Barto, §9.4). Train on experience collected another way, though, and the weights can grow without bound (§11.2), which is a surprisingly nasty failure for a plain weighted sum.

Neural networks go one step further and learn the features too. The parameters are still shared, so interference and moving targets come along with them. DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) adds the two stabilizers in ⑤. There's also a question hiding in that replay memory: the policy that generated the stored transitions can differ from the policy the targets evaluate. That's the on-policy versus off-policy split, and it feeds straight into the deadly triad. So whenever a table becomes a learned function, I'd ask two things about the features: which states do they make look identical, and which other predictions does one update move?

The updates in symbols

For transition t, St is the current state, Rt+1 the reward after the action, wt the current weights, γ the discount and α the step size. The target is yt = Rt+1 + γv̂(St+1, wt), with the successor value set to 0 at a terminal state. The per-transition loss is Lt(w) = ½[yt − v̂(St, w)]², with yt held constant during differentiation. With δt = yt − v̂(St, wt), the update is wt+1 = wt + αδt∇wv̂(St, wt). In the linear case the gradient is x(St). Because the target is recomputed after each change to w, no single unchanged loss holds for the whole run.

DQN works with action values. Qθ(s, a) is the live network's estimate of the value of taking action a in state s, and θ are its weights. θ̄ are the target network's weights, which stay constant between scheduled copies from θ. The live estimate is fit to zt = Rt+1 + γ maxa′ Qθ̄(St+1, a′), where a′ ranges over the actions available in the next state St+1 and the max picks the highest-valued one. At a terminal transition, zt = Rt+1. Frozen θ̄ still gives different targets for different sampled transitions.

Sources: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, §§9.1 to 9.4 and 11.2. Mnih et al., 2015, Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning.
